text:
Data points to mull as the US markets reached an all time high and US yields also reached a high.

The Nasdaq hit an all-time high of 27,773 as the 10-year Treasury yield reached a 20-year high of 5.3%. Equities are pricing a massive AI-driven earnings boom. Bonds are pricing inflation, fiscal tightening, deficits, and macro uncertainty. Are stocks looking through a short-term capex cycle to a structural shift, and an economic revolution driven by AI? Are bonds still focused on the cycle?

The Nasdaq-100 is expected to grow earnings about 45–50% over the next 12 months. Most of that growth is concentrated. Chips and memory are about a third of the index’s value, but about 77% of the promised earnings growth. Nvidia alone is about 28% of it, and Micron about 21%. Strip those groups out and the rest of the index is expected to grow earnings by about 16%.

That brings us to Nvidia. For most of the past three decades, the largest U.S. company has been about 1–3% of total market cap, with a few exceptions, rising toward 6–7% since 2020. Nvidia alone is about $5.8 trillion, or 7–8% of a U.S. market near $77 trillion. Apple, Alphabet, and Microsoft add another large slice. The top 10 companies are now about $31 trillion, roughly 40% of the U.S. market. A handful of technology firms now account for a bigger share of U.S. market value than General Electric, Exxon Mobil, or even peak-bubble Intel ever did.

The Buffett indicator — total U.S. stock-market value divided by GDP — is about 236–239%. Equities near $77 trillion against expected 2026 nominal GDP of about $32.5 trillion means the market is worth more than twice the economy. In a 2001 Fortune piece, Buffett called this ratio probably the best single measure of valuations, and said that as it approaches 200%, as it did in late 1999 and early 2000, investors are “playing with fire.” Today’s reading is above that line, and above the dot-com peak on the same measure.

One offset is foreign earnings. Mega-cap companies earn a large share of their profits abroad, which pushes the ratio up over time, and they are not all trading at astronomical multiples of those earnings.

Conclusion: Stocks and bonds are telling different stories. Equities are pricing an AI earnings boom led by a few chipmakers and probably also the next leg of cascading effects. Bonds are pricing tighter money and fiscal strain or possibly are also looking at higher long term growth. The higher yields, concentration risk and elevated market / GDP ratios do indicate a bumpy ride ahead, even as AI disrupts and marches ahead with leaps rather than baby steps, unleashing a new era. In the meanwhile, vigilant strategies to ride the roller coaster, that likely will reach new peaks eventually. $NVDA  #nasdaq #AI

text:
The Implied Royalty Rate of Taction’s Patent Damages Award

$5.7 billion is a massive, crooked number that a California jury awarded Taction Technology for Apple's patent infringement of haptic technology.

Apple losing a massive patent litigation case is not surprising. Apple has a well-documented history of patent infringement.

Some experts have suggested that an iPhone contains over 250,000 (1) different patented inventions. The vast majority of those inventions were not created by Apple. Still, most experts believe the Federal Circuit will dramatically reduce the $5.7 billion damages award, but the question remains: How did the jury get to that figure?

A quick inquiry into the total number of accused products suggests Apple sold about 1.6 billion devices that use Taction's patents from 2021 through September 2026. Based on the $5.7 billion award, that suggests an implied royalty rate of $3.54 per iPhone and Apple Watch sold, globally (2).

As a percentage of revenue, Apple’s device revenue that used Taction’s patents was close to $1.3 trillion over the same period, implying a 0.47% royalty rate.

Apple’s Two Paths

Taction is a technology innovator specializing in enhanced haptics for electronic devices. "Haptics" refers to the science of enabling interaction with technology through touch. Founded in 2014 by Dr. Silmon James Biggs, Taction's first product was launched in 2016, but it did not become a meaningful branded product.

So what does an inventive innovator and entrepreneur do when their products fail to launch but their inventions are broadly used by larger companies with established market traction?

Create a patent and IP licensing program, of course. That is what Taction and hundreds of other companies pivot toward when they can't gain the market traction they hoped for. And they did it. Taction signed a patent-licensing deal with Corsair that allowed the licensee to sell a pair of headphones that used Taction's patents.

In 2020, Apple could have in-licensed the patented technology. Taction was only a six-year-old company that needed income or investment to survive. Taction had two paths: an easy road or a hard road. Apple could have helped them take the easy road. Instead, Apple and Taction took the hard road.

The easy road would have required a willing licensee, Apple, to respect the inventions created by Taction and make a good-faith licensing offer. The hard road, which Taction took, was to find a litigation funder (Burford Capital) and litigate for infringement.

In the easy-road scenario, Apple would have reviewed the patents Taction created, recognized the evidence of use, and made a licensing offer. A reasonable offer might have been $25 million upfront and $0.25 per device.

In that scenario, Apple would have paid about $430 million in patent licensing fees. Instead, because Taction took the hard road, Apple is on the hook for $5.7 billion.

The difference is a $0.25 royalty rate compared with the implied royalty rate from the jury verdict of $3.54 per product (+/- $0.25).

Most patent experts would likely agree that $3.54 per device for two patents is high, but at $0.25 per device, it starts to make sense from an apportionment standpoint.

Apportionment is a critical input to determining a reasonable royalty relative to the technology it provides. No one is better positioned to calculate apportionment than the product commercializer. But they rarely do, and when they do, they keep the pricing terms confidential.

If Apple cares about other people’s IP, they’ll settle this out rather than wait for the Federal Circuit's appeal ruling. I don't know anyone at Taction, but I suspect they’ll be willing to listen to a reasonable settlement offer.

=======================================

Notes:

(1) The 250,000 patents estimate is not based on an actual technical review of an iPhone. No one has ever made a public technical assessment of how many patented technologies exist in an iPhone.

(2) The patent litigation case is about two US patents. If the implied royalty rate for the damages awarded is calculated on US devices only, it exceeds $9 per device.

→ 全程由 Pi Agent 完成，在 Muse 的任务面板里能看到每一步，用的全是免费额度

text:
I met Matan Angrest at the Rebbe's Ohel. Like many of the other freed hostages I've stood there with, he'd come to thank G-d.

He told me that in captivity he demanded a siddur, a Chumash and a pair of tefillin. And eventually, his captors gave them to him.

He said, "I prayed three times a day, morning, afternoon and night. It protected me. It gave me hope."

I don't know another people that asks to pray in such darkness.

I don't know another people that, after everything we've gone through, packs the shuls even more.

I don't know another people that, after horrors like that, runs to wear its Judaism even more openly.

That's the power of a Jew. You can hold his body captive, and his soul still reaches for G-d. Our enemies never understood that.

Three years ago, they thought they could scare us. Come to a Chabad House on Friday night and try to find a seat.

They thought our kids would hide on campus. Walk down a dorm hallway and see the mezuzos.

They thought we'd try to blend in. Today, more and more young Jews are realizing dating Jewish is not optional.

And it's not just a feeling. An independent survey found that close to half of all the Jews reconnecting since October 7th are doing it through Chabad.

So this October 7th, take on one more mitzvah. A mezuzah, Shabbos candles, Friday night at Chabad, whatever it is for you.

The Rebbe taught us that strong, positive action is the only response. They tried to tear us down. We build.

text:
More than 2 years ago, I didn’t know how to build software.

I just knew AI was going to change everything.

When I first realized ChatGPT could write code, something clicked:

Maybe I could finally build the ideas that had always been stuck in my head.

So I started.

My first major project was PXLWorld, a platform for finding creative jobs across the internet.

I taught myself databases, workflows, servers, Cloudflare, Supabase, GitHub, deployment and more.

Mostly by asking AI questions, copying code, breaking things… and figuring out why they broke. 

😂

That taught me an important lesson early:

Context is everything.

I kept building.

Eventually PXLWorld became an AI image/video platform with GPU infrastructure and automated generation pipelines.

A LOT of late nights went into it.

But I also learned something else:

Building a product and building a business are two completely different things.

The problem matters.

Distribution matters.

The customer matters.

Then AI agents changed everything for me.

For the first time, AI wasn’t just giving me code.

It could actually work inside my infrastructure.

Eventually I found Hermes and integrated it into GitHub, Cloudflare, Supabase, my servers, databases and business knowledge.

Today the way I build looks completely different.

I guide.

My agent builds.

I test.

We iterate.

When I talk with a client, I can record the conversation, transcribe it, and Atlas, my agent, helps turn that conversation into an actual plan for what we should build.

Then we build it.

It still blows my mind.

But it took me years of failures, rebuilding and experimenting to get here.

I don’t think everyone should have to go through that same learning curve.

So I’m opening an AI Agent Launchpad for 10 people.

This isn’t a course about better prompts.

It’s about learning how to actually build with an agent.

How to give it context.

How to connect tools.

How to create guardrails.

How to integrate it into your business.

How to make AI actually DO things. (and it can do ANYTHING)

And I’ll open up BuildWithPXL so you can see how I’ve built my own system.

If you keep thinking:

“I know AI can do more… I just don’t know how to build it.”

This is for you.

👉 https://t.co/mmeBqnEXYC

10 people.

Small group.

Hands-on.

Let’s build something.

text:
OUR NEW SHORT: $PRG

We are short PROG Holdings Inc. (PRG), a US consumer finance company with a $2bn enterprise value and three key business units. Below is a summary of some of our forensic analysis and opinions about this company; for the full short thesis, including endnotes and our very important disclaimer about our financial interests and how they work, please see the Jehoshaphat Research website.

1) In our opinion, the opportunity to be short PRG exists mainly because of desperate underwriting and accounting actions taken by Management that are obscuring weakening demand in each of its three main business units. This has prevented analysts and investors from becoming aware of these problems (and led to misguided valuation analyses of PRG). The stock has few skeptics today, with little short interest and virtually no negative sell-side coverage.

2) PRG’s “crown jewel” business is Four, its highly valued BNPL property to which investors ascribe around half of the stock’s intrinsic value in sum-of-the-parts analyses. We have concluded that Four is playing games with its credit loss accounting; that these accounting games are being used to cover up increasingly desperate underwriting; and that this desperate underwriting in turn has been implemented to obscure falling underlying demand growth. Notably, the beginning of all these desperate actions appears to coincide with Four’s Co-Founder and CEO both leaving the company in 2025. We expect Four to negatively surprise investors on both credit losses and revenues due to its accounting aggression, underwriting changes, and misunderstood unit economics. The PRG bull case, which rests so heavily on Four, will be neutralized by shortcomings in this business unit alone.

3) PRG bought Purchasing Power for $0.4bn this year and has led investors to believe that it is a “low-double-digit” growth business. Based on interviews with former employees and document analysis, we conclude that Purchasing Power is more like a +2-3% grower that has been decelerating for many years, a perpetual disappointment to its former owners, and apparently a negative surprise to PRG after buying it. We believe that PRG has effectively misrepresented Purchasing Power’s past, present, and likely future performance and therefore will not achieve ambitious consensus expectations for it. Purchasing Power also has some surprising revenue dis-synergies with its new owner, meaning the business will likely struggle to achieve even its historical low-single-digit growth; let alone the low-double-digit nonsense modeled by the Street.

4) PRG’s legacy business is Progressive Leasing, a lease-to-own business in chronic decline. We believe this decline is intensifying at a particularly inconvenient time, when the Street is expecting an acceleration to sustained organic growth as high as 5% annually in this business unit. Progressive has attempted to offset these problems through overly loose underwriting, which it is just now pulling back from out of necessity; such tightening may “right-size” the business eventually, but we believe it will make it virtually impossible to hit Street expectations. The underlying problem at the Progressive Leasing business seems to be a groundswell of new competition from better-positioned alternatives, and our field research suggests that one result of this competition is that Progressive is being “demoted” by retail partners left and right while paying more to keep the ones it has. All of this is already happening, but on the horizon, Progressive Leasing – which relies on its size, retailer relationships, and brand to win business – is one of the consumer finance companies most vulnerable to would-be customers asking AI agents to choose the best deal, period, for them at the checkout counter.

We always leave some of the more interesting things for readers of the full report, so we encourage you to visit our website and download the PDF of our short thesis, paying attention as well to our very important disclaimer. Comments and corrections welcome at our website or our email address.

Super excited to finally release @Faradex_ai to the world. We’ve just wrapped up a several-month pilot with around a dozen enterprise firms across healthcare, insurance, wealth management, legal, and more. 

We started Faradex after struggling to find a solution for truly secure and confidential AI. 

I was running multiple workflows a day on a traditional Claude account, knowing that my data was sitting on shared servers and that unless I had an enterprise account, my chats were actively being used for training. 

After looking into the enterprise plans of several leading frontier models, a few things became super clear… zero data retention (ZDR) doesn’t actually mean zero, small firms are being left behind with no support and 20-seat minimums, and quite literally everyone is doing it. Everyone is uploading confidential data, and they know they shouldn’t be. 

So stop. Check out https://t.co/GMcUXh8ZuW and launch a secure, fully private AI instance in minutes. 

Or at least like and share this if you see it :)

text:
Day 2 of how we built DevBox, our internal coding agent. This one is about where the agent actually runs. 🧵

The agent runs arbitrary code as root, so we needed real isolation. We also needed Docker + Compose for integration tests, our own network policy, and to run on our own Kubernetes, near our data.

We looked at hosted sandbox providers like E2B, Daytona and Modal. For some, Docker support was still experimental. We also wanted strict path-based control over network egress and flexible credential injection that supports rotation. E2B was the closest fit but did not meet that last requirement.

So we picked OpenSandbox, self-hosted on our EKS cluster. Each sandbox is a pod running inside a Kata Containers microVM.

That VM is the security boundary. Inside it, the agent gets full access: no approval prompts, no nested sandboxing. We trust the box.

The agent runs arbitrary code as root, so we needed real isolation. We also needed Docker + Compose for integration tests, our own network policy, and to run on our own Kubernetes, near our data.

We looked at hosted sandbox providers like E2B, Daytona and Modal. For some, Docker support was still experimental. We also wanted strict path-based control over network egress and flexible credential injection that supports rotation. E2B was the closest fit but did not meet that last requirement.

So we picked OpenSandbox, self-hosted on our EKS cluster. Each sandbox is a pod running inside a Kata Containers microVM.

That VM is the security boundary. Inside it, the agent gets full access: no approval prompts, no nested sandboxing. We trust the box.

I'm 14 and I sent over 450 cold emails trying to land website clients.

Here is what gets a reply:

1. Take the time to write a well thought out email. It will show up in the results.

2. Follow up on the same thread. This got me 50% of replies. 

3. Target local businesses. People have a higher chance of responding if you are local.

4. Have your portfolio ready to send. Most replies were asking for a list of sites I had already done.

5. Show where you could provide value.

Your success in cold outreach depends on how you iterate.

Try leaving TwinMind on all day on your phone, watch, Mac or Windows and share the coolest workflows you can build with this!
